opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, the connection is actually pretty direct. A lot of what we did with AI Snake Oil was trying to separate the things that genuinely work from the things that are being sold on the basis of claims that don't hold up. And one of the recurring patterns we kept running into was that the gap between hype and reality very often lives in the evaluation. Somebody reports an impressive number on a benchmark, and that number gets translated in press releases and headlines into a claim about real-world capability that the benchmark was never designed to support.

With agents, that problem gets dramatically worse. When you're evaluating a language model on, say, a question-answering benchmark, there's at least a relatively well-defined input and output. With agents, you've got multi-step interactions, tool use, environments that can change, and costs that can vary enormously depending on how many times the agent calls the model or retries. So when we started looking at agent evaluations, we found a lot of the same issues we'd been flagging in other contexts, just amplified.

A few concrete things stood out. One is cost. Many agent leaderboards report accuracy alone, but you can often boost accuracy just by throwing more compute at the problem, running the model many times, retrying, voting. If you don't report cost alongside accuracy, you can't tell whether a fancy new agent architecture is actually better or just more expensive. In some of our work, simple baselines that were much cheaper matched or beat elaborate agent designs once you accounted for that. So we've argued pretty strongly that agent evaluations should be cost-controlled, essentially looking at a Pareto frontier of accuracy versus cost rather than a single number.

Another issue is the difference between what model developers need and what downstream users need. A researcher might want to know about the frontier of capability, but someone deciding whether to deploy an agent cares about reliability and cost in their specific setting. Those are different evaluation questions, and conflating them leads to misleading conclusions.

Then there's overfitting and shortcuts. Benchmarks often don't have proper holdout sets, or the holdouts don't reflect the kind of generalization you'd actually need. Agents can learn to exploit quirks of the benchmark rather than solve the underlying task. That's very much the same story we told in AI Snake Oil about predictive AI: something looks great in the lab and then falls apart in deployment.

And finally, reproducibility. We found that a lot of agent evaluation results were hard to reproduce, partly because of non-standardized harnesses and partly because small implementation details make a big difference. That's part of why we've put effort into more standardized evaluation infrastructure.

So I'd say the through-line is a kind of skepticism that I hope is constructive. The point isn't that agents don't work or that AI is all hype. It's that if we want to know what actually works, we have to be really careful about how we measure it, and right now a lot of the measurement isn't up to the job of supporting the claims being made.

r001.rationale: The response directly connects AI Snake Oil’s critique of unsupported claims to agent evaluations, applying the same skepticism to benchmark claims and recommending cost-aware, reliable, reproducible measurement.

r002.rationale: It discusses real-world capability, deployment needs, reliability, and cost, but frames better evaluations as a way to measure what works and assess claims. It does not identify improved real-world agent performance as the goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the book and the agent evaluation work come from the same place, which is a frustration with the gap between what gets claimed and what actually holds up when you look carefully.

In AI Snake Oil, Sayash Kapoor and I spent a lot of time on predictive AI, where the pattern was that a tool would be sold as predicting who would commit a crime or who would succeed at a job, and when you looked under the hood the evaluation was either nonexistent or deeply flawed. Often the thing being measured wasn't the thing that mattered. That trained us to ask a few reflexive questions: what exactly was evaluated, by whom, under what conditions, and does that bear any relationship to the setting where the system will actually be deployed?

When we turned to agents, we saw the same dynamics playing out, just faster and with more money behind them. Someone announces an agent that scored X on some benchmark, and that gets reported as "AI can now do your job." But when we dug into how agents were being evaluated, we found a lot of problems. Benchmarks didn't account for cost, so an agent that called the model fifty times to squeeze out a slightly higher accuracy looked strictly better than a cheaper one. There was a lot of overfitting, where agents were essentially tuned to the quirks of a particular benchmark and had shortcuts baked in that would never transfer. Holdout sets were often inadequate or didn't exist. And reproducibility was poor enough that we sometimes couldn't even confirm the headline numbers.

So the book informed the research in a very direct way. It gave us a checklist of failure modes to look for, and it gave us a disposition, which is that the burden of proof should be on the person making the claim. It also shaped what we think good evaluation looks like. We've argued that agent benchmarks should report cost alongside accuracy, that they should be designed with the downstream use in mind rather than as leaderboard games, and that developers and evaluators should be more candid about what the benchmark does and doesn't tell you.

The other thing I'd say is that the book made us careful not to overcorrect. Skepticism about hype is not the same as dismissing the technology. Agents are genuinely useful in some settings, and the point of better evaluation isn't to debunk them, it's to figure out where they actually work so people can make reasonable decisions. If anything, I think the hype is bad for the field because it erodes trust that the real successes depend on.

r001.rationale: The response says AI Snake Oil supplied a checklist of evaluation failure modes and a burden-of-proof stance, then applies them to rigorous agent benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It calls for evaluating agents with downstream use in mind rather than as leaderboard games, to identify where they actually work and support reasonable decisions.

astra-6.text:
I see them as closely connected. A lot of the work of AI Snake Oil is asking: What evidence would actually justify this claim? And with agents, that becomes a very concrete research question. If an agent performs well on a benchmark, what have we learned about its ability to do useful work in the real world?

There’s a gap between showing that something can succeed on a task and showing that it can do so reliably, at an acceptable cost, under the conditions where people will actually use it. An impressive demonstration can establish the first without telling us much about the second.

So that perspective pushes us to examine the evaluation itself. Are we measuring the capability we care about? Are we accounting for how much money and computation the agent uses? Does the result hold when we vary the task or the environment? And are we giving other researchers enough information to reproduce it?

The goal is to make the evidence more useful. Better evaluations should help us distinguish real progress from improvements that look impressive on a leaderboard but don’t translate into practical value.

r001.rationale: The response applies AI Snake Oil’s focus on what evidence justifies a claim to agent evaluations, calling for evaluation of relevant capabilities, costs, varied conditions, and reproducibility.

r002.rationale: It says evaluations should establish whether agents can do useful work reliably in real-world conditions, beyond success on a benchmark, and distinguish leaderboard gains from practical value.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as closely connected. A lot of the work of AI Snake Oil is asking: What exactly is the claim being made, and does the evidence actually support it? With agents, that leads directly to questions about evaluation. When we say an agent can perform a task, what conditions was it tested under? How much did it cost? How much human intervention did it need? And how reliably does it succeed across repeated attempts?

A benchmark score can be useful, but it’s easy to turn that score into a much broader claim about what a system can do. An agent succeeding in a controlled environment doesn’t automatically tell us whether it will be useful in a real workflow, where the inputs are messy and mistakes have consequences.

So the constructive side of calling out hype is figuring out what better evidence would look like. Can we design evaluations that help someone decide whether to use an agent, understand its limitations, and compare it with simpler alternatives? That’s the connection for me: moving from questioning claims to building ways to test them.

r001.rationale: It connects AI Snake Oil’s scrutiny of evidence behind claims to designing evaluations that test agents’ capabilities, costs, reliability, and human-intervention needs.

r002.rationale: It says benchmark success in a controlled environment does not establish usefulness in real workflows, and frames better evaluations as helping people judge whether to use an agent there.
